title: Guild-Issued Credentials That Beat Free Badges
one_liner: Turn illustrator, photographer, translator and indie-label associations into verifiers that issue portable 'real working creator' credentials.
customer: Trade associations, unions and guilds with 1,000-50,000 members who need visible AI-era member value. Second-side buyers are contests, publishers, agencies and brands that want to check a creator quickly.
problem: Insiders assume a universal proof-of-personhood is needed, like World's iris scans or platform badges. But Spotify says over 99% of artists listeners search for are already verified, so a free badge says nothing about who is a working professional. The brief flags that a paid credential must beat the free native one, and it cannot do so on 'is human' alone.
solution: A white-label service where the guild verifies members using its own dues records and portfolio review, and we issue portable credentials. These are W3C verifiable credentials, Bluesky trusted-verifier labels, a signed .well-known file for members' websites and an embeddable badge. A lookup API lets buyers and contest platforms verify membership and standing. Guilds also get a public directory.
why_now: Org-issued verification became a working pattern on Bluesky in 2025, and TikTok joining C2PA in Jul 2026 shows provenance moving to the mainstream. Guild members are demanding concrete AI-era protection, and platform badges are free and universal, so they cannot signal professional standing.
revenue_model: Association license of $5-25k/year, $1-3 per member per year for issuance, and lookup fees for enterprise buyers such as contests and agencies.
non_obvious_insight: The value of verification comes from the stakes and scarcity of the issuer, not from cryptography. Guilds already own the membership record and the trust, and a platform that gives everyone a badge cannot compete with that.
first_30_days: Pitch 20 mid-size associations with a one-page offer: a 3-week pilot of 100 verified members on Bluesky and their own websites. Charge a $2-5k pilot fee, and aim to have one association make it a renewal benefit.

title: Special-Tool Exchange for Retiring Regional Fleets
one_liner: Buy or take on consignment the OEM special tooling stranded when regionals retire 50-seat jets and older turboprops, calibrate it, and rent or sell it to operators who cannot get it from the OEM for months.
customer: MROs and Part 145 shops adding a regional-jet or turboprop type, Part 135 and cargo operators, freighter-conversion programs, and operators in Latin America, Africa and Asia flying older regional types. Sellers are regional airlines and lessors with tooling cages to empty.
problem: Every type needs OEM special tooling: rigging pins, wing and gear jack adapters, engine sling adapters, pinning tools, pressure-test rigs, borescope adapters, prop and control-rigging fixtures. New from the OEM this is expensive and lead times can run to months, and some tooling is out of production. When a regional retires a subfleet, that tooling is on the tool-control ledger at near-zero book value, taking up cage space. It gets scrapped, shipped out with airframes, or forgotten. Buyers who are desperate for it have no idea the seller exists, and vice versa.
solution: A consignment marketplace and rental pool. Take tooling in from retiring fleets at no cash outlay, on a 70/30 split of sales and rentals. Inspect it, get it recalibrated through a metrology lab, tag it with a certificate, and catalog it with photos and drawing references. Rent it weekly or monthly with a deposit and freight, or sell it. Offer starter tooling bundles for a shop taking on a new type, such as everything needed for a first C-check on that airframe.
why_now: Majors keep replacing 50-seat regional jets and older turboprops with larger regional aircraft, so tooling cages empty every quarter. Cargo conversions and second-life operators in emerging markets are keeping the old types flying. OEM lead times and parts availability have been poor across the industry since 2022, so buyers will pay to skip the wait.
revenue_model: Consignment split on sales, rental fees at roughly 3-6% of replacement value per month, calibration and freight margin, and bundle pricing for new-type start-ups. Later, a subscription for shops that want guaranteed access to a tooling pool.
non_obvious_insight: Tooling has none of the obsolescence problem of parts. It does not expire except for calibration. A directors of maintenance would rather give it away than pay to store it, and nobody knows who the buyers are. The unusual thing about this business is that the inventory is almost free and the demand is urgent, because a missing pin can ground an airplane for weeks.
first_30_days: Call 20 directors of maintenance, tech-services managers and lessor technical reps whose subfleets are winding down. Get two or three tool cages on consignment with no upfront cash. Photograph and catalog them, send calibrated items to a local metrology lab, and publish a simple catalog with rental terms and a deposit process. Contact freighter-conversion programs, Part 135 operators and international MROs that fly the same type. The first rental should close within weeks, because the urgency price is high.

title: Investor-Cap Look-Through Checks for Title Companies
one_liner: An API that traces a buyer's LLC web to its parent and counts the homes it controls, so title and escrow can clear the ROAD Act's 350-home limit at closing.
customer: Title and escrow companies, closing attorneys and lenders in single-family-heavy metros. Secondary: mid-size investors (100-349 homes) who need to stay under the cap and prove it.
problem: The ROAD Act bars investors with more than 350 homes from buying existing houses. Compliance depends on affiliate holdings scattered across thousands of LLCs, which the closing agent cannot see. Large buyers will restructure into fragments, and mid-size investors suddenly need to manage headroom. Who is liable when a closing clears wrongly is unresolved.
solution: Entity resolution across county deed records, Secretary of State filings, registered-agent and address graphs and mailing addresses. It returns a portfolio count with a confidence score in seconds, an audit-ready evidence file for the closing, and a headroom dashboard for investors near the cap. Verify statute text, effective date, affiliate definition and exemptions first.
why_now: The law took effect in July 2026, and implementation questions are open now. Title agents are the natural chokepoint, as they already collect ownership details on entity purchases. Entity-resolution tooling and cheaper county record access make a small-team build feasible.
revenue_model: $15-40 per buyer-entity check. $500-2,000 per month SaaS for investors. Enterprise licenses to title underwriters.
non_obvious_insight: The people obligated to comply cannot compute the answer, and the people who can compute it are not in the transaction. The closing desk becomes the enforcement point, and mid-size investors treat their 350th home as a scarce budget, creating a second buyer for the same data.
first_30_days: Build for three metros where large single-family operators concentrate. Ingest deed and Secretary of State data. Sell paid pilots to 5 title agencies and 2 underwriters. Publish a free entity-count explainer to attract inbound.

title: Compliance-as-Code for EWA and BNPL
one_liner: State-by-state earned wage access and BNPL rules are being written fast. Turn them into an API that checks fees, tips and disclosures before each product release.
customer: EWA and BNPL providers, payroll platforms and neobanks adding these features, and employers running EWA programs.
problem: Colorado sued EarnIn (2026-09-08), Maryland banned EWA tipping, and New York and Illinois have BNPL rules. Each state differs on fees, tips, disclosures and licensing. Product managers ship copy and fee configs faster than lawyers can review them.
solution: A rules engine and configuration API. Providers submit product configs (fees, tip prompts, speed, limits) and get per-state pass/fail, required disclosure text, and a change log. It also monitors new bills and enforcement actions and produces exam-ready evidence.
why_now: Enforcement began in Sept 2026 and legislatures are still moving. Providers need pre-release checks now and will need audit trails when examiners arrive.
revenue_model: $3k-$10k per month per provider, with per-state add-ons and content licensing to law firms.
non_obvious_insight: EWA's legal risk sits in UI copy and fee configuration, which product teams change weekly. Rules-as-code plugs into release management, which a law-firm memo never can.
first_30_days: Publish a free 12-state EWA and BNPL rule tracker as a lead magnet. Pair with a fintech law firm and pitch five mid-size providers and payroll platforms on a $3k per month pilot.

title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.

title: Do-Not-Transact Registry: GAMSTOP for Scams
one_liner: An opt-in registry, controlled by consumers and their families, that crypto ATMs, gift-card sellers and wire desks must check before completing a high-risk transaction.
customer: Crypto-ATM operators and gift-card retailers (paying per check and for legal cover). People enroll for free through credit unions, senior centers and adult children.
problem: Crypto-ATM fraud losses rose 58% to $389M in 2025, 66% of it from victims aged 60+. Older adults lost $7.7B overall. Education campaigns fail because scammers coach victims mid-scam to bypass warnings. State AGs have sued major kiosk operators, and cities are considering bans.
solution: People (or a family member with their consent) register commitments made while calm: no cash-to-crypto, no gift cards above $X, no new-payee wires above $Y, bound to ID number and phone. Kiosks that already scan IDs, and retailers via API at gift-card purchase, check the registry and show a neutral refusal script. Lifting a block takes a 72-hour cooling-off period, which breaks the scammer's urgency.
why_now: State kiosk laws (daily caps, mandatory warnings, refunds) and AG lawsuits give operators an urgent need to prove diligence. IC3's 2025 data quantified the elder-loss concentration. Operators may soon need a defensible control to keep their licenses.
revenue_model: About $0.05-0.25 per check plus $500-2K per month per operator. Gift-card processors and retail chains by contract. Grants and credit-union sponsorships fund enrollment.
non_obvious_insight: UK self-exclusion for gambling works because people commit in a calm moment. Scam prevention has assumed you can persuade people mid-scam, which fails. A registry turns consumer protection into a B2B compliance lookup that operators buy for legal cover, so the payer is not the person at risk.
first_30_days: Build an enrollment page and a kiosk-check API. Pilot with one independent operator (100-500 kiosks) and one state credit-union league, and enroll the first 1,000 people through a credit union or senior center. Use the results to brief state legislators and the AG's office.

title: Tele-Operated Night Aides for Small Care Homes
one_liner: Metered remote-aide hours operating an off-the-shelf mobile manipulator robot in 6-16 bed residential care homes, so labor crosses borders when workers cannot.
customer: Owners of small residential care homes and assisted living homes (adult family homes, RCFEs) that run one awake overnight staffer, paying about $2,500-4,000 a month per home.
problem: Staffing is collapsing, with a 75-country visa pause, Haitian TPS loss and Wisconsin homes closing wings. One Wisconsin operator spent $100k+ on housing for overseas workers and then lost visa access. Small homes cannot buy robots or hire tech staff, and much aide time is walking, fetching and watching.
solution: Lease a wheeled mobile-manipulator (for example a Hello Robot Stretch-class unit) and pair it with remote aides, offshore or US-based. The remote aide handles night rounds, door and light tasks, supply fetching and two-way calming talk with dementia residents. The aide escalates to the on-site caregiver through a shared protocol. Do not touch medication or personal care.
why_now: Teleoperated home robots (1X NEO, Waymo-style remote centers) proved the model in 2025-26. Workers can no longer be moved, but work can. Occupancy is at a 19-year high with no new supply before 2030.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription per home covering robot lease plus a pool of remote hours. Overage billed per hour. Target unit margin of about 40% after remote-labor cost.
non_obvious_insight: Staffing rules count bodies on site, but most overnight risk is watching and fetching, which a remote human plus a modest robot can cover. The visa crackdown turns labor arbitrage into a physical-presence product.
first_30_days: Sign three care homes in one state that allow tech-augmented overnight staffing. Buy one robot and hire two remote aides. Run supervised night shifts and log fall and wandering response times as proof for the next 20 sales.

title: Fuel Surcharge Autopilot for Route-Based Services
one_liner: An add-on for field-service software that adds a transparent, index-linked, capped and self-expiring fuel line to invoices, and explains it to customers.
customer: Small route-based service businesses with 3-50 trucks: lawn and landscape, pest control, pool service, septic and portable toilets, HVAC and plumbing, mobile detailing and small waste haulers. They pay a monthly fee.
problem: Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 from a year ago, and gasoline is $4.48. Large firms absorb it. Cintas says 'we do not pass through any fuel surcharges', and Darden says sustained $6+ diesel would add 10-15 bps of cost. Small operators eat the increase or raise base prices and lose customers, because a surcharge added ad hoc looks like a scam.
solution: A plug-in for Jobber, Housecall Pro, Service Autopilot, Workiz and QuickBooks. The owner sets a base fuel price and a mileage-per-job model, and the plug-in computes a per-visit surcharge from the weekly EIA regional diesel or gasoline index. It adds a labelled invoice line with a cap, sends a one-time customer notice using tested wording, auto-reduces the charge when prices fall, and shows the owner recovered margin. The customer sees a public methodology page.
why_now: The Iran-conflict fuel shock has been running since spring, with diesel up 74% year over year, and it now appears in every large company's guidance (Darden, KB Home, General Mills, AutoZone, Stitch Fix). Small service businesses have had months of margin erosion and lack the pricing staff that large companies use.
revenue_model: $19-$49/month per business, or a 3-5% share of surcharge dollars collected. Add an annual 'fuel and route cost' benchmark report for FSM platforms as a lead generator.
non_obvious_insight: Fuel is a trust problem, not a math problem. The EIA shows diesel at $6.529/gal on Sept 21, 2026, up $2.780 year over year, with gasoline at $4.478 (https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/). Cintas's CEO says 'it's a volatile situation with the price at the pump. We do not pass through any fuel surcharges' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/cintas-ctas-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). Darden's CFO puts the risk from sustained elevated diesel at 10-15 bps of sales and says its delivery fees sit in fixed-price contracts (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/darden-dri-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). H.B. Fuller says small and mid-sized customers' order patterns swing on oil headlines (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/fuller-ful-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Small operators cannot afford the customer backlash that large companies can, so a public formula, a cap and an automatic expiry are the product. Field-service platforms have not built this. The risk is that Jobber or ServiceTitan ship it natively, so the plan is to sell to the operator through a marketplace listing first and move quickly.
first_30_days: Build a minimal version as a Jobber integration or a Zapier plus Google Sheets tool driven by the EIA diesel API. Post in landscaping, pest and pool operator communities (Facebook groups, r/lawncare, LawnSite, PCT forums) offering a free tool and template customer letter. Get 20 operators to run it for one billing cycle, measure surcharge acceptance and cancellations, then start charging $29/month. Apply to the Jobber and Housecall Pro app marketplaces in parallel.

title: Substitute-Plan Binders for Retiring Business Owners
one_liner: Retired teachers interview 60+ owner-operators and write a 'sub plan' any stranger could use to run the shop for a week, sold through business brokers.
customer: Owner-operators aged 60+ of $300k-$3M revenue businesses that depend on the owner's head (HVAC and plumbing, vet and dental practices, hardware stores, salons, daycares, landscaping). The channel and co-payer is the business broker, plus SBA lenders, CPAs and estate attorneys. Acquirers such as search-fund and ETA buyers pay later for a 'day-one' version.
problem: About 40% of small business owners are boomers, and roughly 6 million businesses will change hands by 2035. Around 70% of listed small businesses never sell, and about half of owners have no succession plan. Buyers and lenders can't underwrite what lives only in the owner's memory. Owners refuse to write SOPs, but they will talk for hours. Brokers watch listings die at the diligence stage because 'the business is the owner.'
solution: Two half-day interview sessions plus a video walk-through of the shop. Teachers are trained to draw knowledge out of people with questions. The output is a 20-40 page Sub Plan written in the classroom genre. It covers the daily schedule and routines, where the keys and passwords are, the 'kids to watch' (the difficult customer, the vendor who needs a call before noon, the employee who needs praise), emergency procedures, a first-hour and first-week script, and 'what NOT to do.' The org chart is drawn as a seating chart showing who actually influences whom. Then comes the sub test. A stranger runs a 4-hour shift from the binder, and every gap they hit gets fixed. The result becomes a diligence exhibit in the sale memorandum. AI transcription and structuring keep labor cost low, and the human elicitation stays the scarce part.
why_now: Coverage of the 'Great Ownership Transfer' peaked in 2026 (McKinsey, Forbes and others). First-time buyers via SBA 7(a) loans and search funds are flooding the market and underwriting transferability. AI transcription and structuring dropped the cost of capturing tacit knowledge by roughly 10x in the last two years. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, and estate attorneys are seeing more 'owner died, business worthless in 90 days' cases.
revenue_model: $2,400 flat per binder, usually rolled into the broker's listing package. Brokers get a referral credit of about $300. There is a $49/month 'living binder' update plan. Buyers can pay $1,500 for a post-close rewrite. There is a $600 add-on for estate attorneys covering an 'if I'm hit by a bus' version.
non_obvious_insight: The sub plan is the most battle-tested knowledge-transfer document in existence. Every teacher has written hundreds of them for a stranger with 30 unpredictable kids and six hours. No consultant has that reps count. The real asset in a small business is the informal 'kids to watch' list, which never appears in any SOP. Sellers don't fail because they lack documents. They fail because nobody asked the right questions in the right order.
first_30_days: Recruit 4-5 retired teachers who like interviewing. Pick one metro and pitch 20 business brokers with one offer: 'give me your stalest listing, the one that has sat 9+ months, and I'll run a free pilot binder.' Do 3 free pilots in exchange for testimonials and an intro to the broker's next 5 listings. Then charge $2,400. Add SCORE chapters, SBDCs and estate attorneys as second-wave channels.

title: Solar Battery Warranty-Claim Recovery Desk
one_liner: Pool failed-battery claims from small African installers and enforce them against Chinese manufacturers for a share of recovered value.
customer: Solar installers and importers in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa holding failed batteries and inverters.
problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panels from China since 2024. Cheap packs fail, and claims need serial verification, BMS logs, RMA logistics and language skills, so installers absorb the losses.
solution: A claims desk that captures failure evidence by QR and app, files with OEMs, consolidates returns and tracks credit notes. The wedge is five Lagos importers with a backlog of dead units.
why_now: The battery import surge of 2024-26 is now reaching failure age, and installer margins are compressing.
revenue_model: 15-25% of recovered value, moving to SaaS plus failure-data sales to insurers.
non_obvious_insight: A warranty is worth only what you can enforce. Batching many small buyers gives leverage over OEMs and produces failure data that insurers need.
first_30_days: Collect backlog lists from three importers and file the first 100 claims.

title: Dialysis Chair-Fill Rides Paid Per Completed Treatment
one_liner: A dedicated, route-based ride service for dialysis patients (same driver, same van loop, three times a week) priced per treatment completed instead of per trip, sold to the clinics and risk-bearing kidney-care companies that lose money on every missed session.
customer: Independent dialysis clinic groups and mid-sized operators worried about chair utilization, plus value-based kidney-care companies and Medicare Advantage ESRD plans that carry the hospitalization cost when a patient misses treatment.
problem: Medicaid non-emergency transport is a low-margin, hated business: pooled dispatch, late or missed pickups, and one-off rides for patients who actually have 156 predictable trips a year. The largest broker, ModivCare, went through Chapter 11 in 2025, so states and payers are unhappy with the incumbent. Meanwhile a missed dialysis session is expensive: in one study about 5% of patients were hospitalized within two days of a missed appointment versus 1.2% of those who attended. Medicare pays the clinic a bundled rate of about $282 per treatment in 2026, so every no-show is lost revenue, an idle chair and staff, and a sicker patient.
solution: Run dialysis like a bus route. Batch patients by chair shift and neighborhood, fix pickup windows, and assign dedicated driver-and-vehicle pairs so the patient sees the same person every time. Add SMS check-in, a same-day fallback ride through a taxi or rideshare partner, and a no-show guarantee. Report completed-treatment rates to the clinic weekly. Price by completed treatment (a round trip in the tens of dollars against roughly $280 of chair revenue), with an upside share for a lower missed-session rate. Structure it inside the Anti-Kickback local-transportation safe harbor, or bill risk-bearing plans and kidney-care companies directly, and confirm that with health-care counsel before launch.
why_now: ModivCare's bankruptcy and its emergence at the end of 2025 left NEMT contracts in flux and states re-examining brokers. CMS's kidney care models and Medicare Advantage special-needs plans are pushing risk onto companies that now feel every hospital day. Federal Medicaid cuts mean clinics and plans need cheaper ways to protect revenue rather than more benefits.
revenue_model: Fee per completed treatment (about $45-$75 round trip depending on wheelchair mix), with a bonus tied to reducing the clinic's missed-treatment rate. Second line: chemo and radiation patients on the same route logic.
non_obvious_insight: A dialysis chair is perishable inventory, like an airline seat, and the ride is a $50 cost that protects a $280 seat-day and a threefold hospitalization risk. NEMT is a terrible business because it treats a predictable, recurring, high-stakes patient as a random one-off trip. Treat those patients as a subscription route and the economics flip from a race to the bottom on price per mile to a premium on reliability.
first_30_days: Sell one independent operator with 3-5 clinics in one metro on a 60-day pilot covering 15-20 patients. Use two leased accessible vans, or subcontract a local NEMT operator, and two salaried drivers. Get the clinic's baseline missed-treatment rate from its own records and agree the target in writing before starting. Charge per completed treatment from day one, then take the data to a kidney-care company or MA plan for a larger contract.

title: Modern Lodges for Fraternal Insurers
one_liner: A Lodge-as-a-Service company that builds young-adult chapters for existing fraternal benefit societies, pairing initiation ritual and mutual aid with their insurance licence.
customer: Fraternal benefit societies (roughly 200 in the US, with about $328B in assets and nearly 8 million members per industry figures) that need younger members, and the millennials and Gen Z members who pay dues.
problem: State law requires fraternal benefit societies to operate through a lodge system with regular meetings and ritual, yet lodge participation and the median member's age have both drifted the wrong way. Meanwhile lonely young adults, especially men, have almost no places built on commitment, mutual aid and belonging, and few own life or disability coverage.
solution: A branded 'new lodge' layer under an existing society's licence: chapters for a specific tribe such as tradespeople, first responders or new fathers. Each has a modern initiation ritual, monthly 'work nights' of volunteer building, a small mutual-aid fund, and a term-life or disability product sold through the society. We provide recruiting, chapter software, ritual scripts and host training.
why_now: The male-loneliness conversation peaked in 2024-26, and run clubs and other third places prove appetite for group belonging. Fraternal insurers hold the capital and the licence but have lost the recruiting engine, and most have never tried a modern chapter model.
revenue_model: Per-member acquisition fee of roughly $200-500, a revenue share of first-year and renewal premium (for example 10-20%), and chapter software and licensing fees per month.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest asset for a startup building community plus mutual aid is an insurance licence, and the scarcest asset for a fraternal insurer is young community. Fraternal law makes ritual and lodges a regulatory requirement, so what looks like cost and cringe to a founder is actually a moat. The two parties need each other and neither can buy the other's asset.
first_30_days: Email membership and innovation directors at 30 mid-sized societies. Launch one pilot lodge in a single city with 25 founding members and a paid 'charter night'. Secure a letter of intent from one society to share premium revenue.

title: Mailed Proof Books for Grandparents Who Buy Prints
one_liner: Turn a wedding gallery into a personalized printed booklet, mailed to each grandparent and parent with a phone number to order prints, because the people who actually pay for wedding prints never click gallery links.
customer: Wedding photographers (they pay only via revenue share). The end payers are the couple's parents, in-laws and grandparents, who spend $150-400 per household on prints and albums.
problem: The dirty secret of studio economics is that couples buy almost nothing after delivery. They have the gallery and Instagram. The people who buy prints and albums are mothers, mothers-in-law and grandparents, and the photographer's only delivery channel is a link emailed to the couple, who rarely forward it. Pic-Time and similar platforms added face-recognition and selfie-search galleries in late 2025, but that assumes a phone-comfortable guest willing to scan their face on a website. Grandma will not do that. Every wedding leaves an estimated $500-2,000 of print revenue uncollected, and the 'last photo with Grandpa' has a clock on it.
solution: The photographer uploads the gallery and the family list (they already have it from the formals shot list). We cluster faces, have the photographer confirm the 6-12 key elders and parents, and auto-build a 16-24 page softcover booklet per person ('Nana's Book: 22 photos of you and your grandkids'). We print and mail it within about 10 days of gallery delivery, with the couple's opt-in and a handwritten-style note from them. Every booklet carries a QR code plus a toll-free number answered first by a human and later by a voice agent that takes orders by phone and card, with check-by-mail as an option. Orders are fulfilled through pro labs, and the photographer sees a dashboard of sales.
why_now: AI face search has just become standard in photographer gallery platforms (Pic-Time's Nov 2025 update), which proves photographers will pay for AI galleries but leaves the elder channel unserved. Softcover print-on-demand now lands at roughly $6-10 for a 24-page book via lab and POD APIs. 2026-grade voice agents can take a print order from a 78-year-old who hates websites. Wedding-guest demographics are also aging, since couples are marrying later and grandparents are still at the table.
revenue_model: No upfront fee to the photographer. We front the booklet cost (about $10 landed) and keep roughly 40% of resulting print and album order revenue at lab retail, with the photographer keeping 60%, which is pure incremental margin. Optional $15 flat per-booklet pricing for photographers who want to buy outright.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the client. The couple's inbox is the wrong channel, and a personalized object with the recipient's own face on it is something people do not throw away. The product is a channel to 60-85-year-olds who respond to paper and phone calls, and the gallery software is just the data source.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 photographers from local and online groups who delivered a wedding in the last 6 months. Produce booklets for 2 of their weddings each, at your cost (about $100 in print and postage per wedding), using a Pic-Time/ShootProof export, open-source face clustering (InsightFace) and a lab or Lulu/Blurb-style API. Route the phone number to the founder's cell. Track orders per booklet. If 1 in 5 booklets converts to a $100+ order, sign the rev-share terms and scale to 50 studios.

title: Orphaned Solar Lease Cleanup at Home Closings
one_liner: A closing-desk service that untangles orphaned solar leases, PPAs and UCC fixture filings on retirees' homes so sales and estates can close.
customer: Title and escrow companies, listing agents, elder-law attorneys and estate executors, who pay per closing (fee taken from sale proceeds). Secondary customers are the retired homeowners themselves and their adult children.
problem: Door-to-door and telemarketed solar leases and PPAs were sold at kitchen tables to retirees on 20-25 year terms. Each one usually leaves a UCC-1 fixture filing on the home. The lessor may since have gone bankrupt (Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 and its portfolio was sold and is now serviced by SunStrong; Mosaic and Sunlight failed earlier). Sales stall at the last minute because the buyer's lender wants the lease assumed or paid off and nobody can find the assignment chain, the current servicer or a payoff quote. Heirs inherit a lease on a dead parent's house, with monitoring dead and inverters failing. Homeowners rarely have copies of what they signed.
solution: A fixed-scope workflow. (1) Pull county and state fixture filings and reconstruct the chain of assignment. (2) Identify the current servicer and pull the contract. (3) Produce either a lender-ready transfer/assumption package with the buyer's credit-approval prep, or a payoff/buyout quote. (4) File the lien release. (5) Where the sales pitch looks deceptive or the lease unenforceable, hand off to a consumer attorney. A shared database of lessor entities, servicers and their turnaround times compounds as more closings run through it. The service is priced so title companies see it as saving their fee on a dying deal.
why_now: The Sunnova bankruptcy (filed June 2025, plan effective November 2025) created a live wave of stuck transfers, and multiple state AGs are investigating. The federal homeowner solar credit ended after 2025, pushing installers toward leases and PPAs, which let the company keep the tax credit. Leases signed in 2016-2020 are now reaching resale and probate age as the peak-65 cohort dies or downsizes.
revenue_model: Flat $750-$1,500 per closing, paid at settlement from proceeds. Title companies can take a $299/month priority-handling subscription. There is an optional buyout-negotiation success fee, and attorney referral fees where the state allows.
non_obvious_insight: The panels are not the blocker. The blocker is paperwork nobody can find: a recorded fixture filing and an assignment chain across three companies. Closers know it as the #1 surprise at the eleventh hour. Half the street signed in 2017 with a clipboard salesman and kept no copies. Whoever owns the lessor and servicer map, and the county filing pipeline, owns the unblock.
first_30_days: Pick one high-solar county in TX, FL, CA or AZ. Scrape recorded fixture filings by known lessors and cross-match them against new listings and probate filings. Call 15 title offices that have had a stuck solar closing and offer the first 3 at cost. Build template packages for the top 5 lessors and servicers. Partner with one elder-law attorney and one consumer-protection lawyer for hand-offs.

title: Phage Red-Teaming and Immunity Stacks for Fermenters
one_liner: Penetration-test production strains with adversarially evolved phages, then harden them with stacked, AI-selected anti-phage defenses.
customer: Industrial fermentation operators and CDMOs running E. coli, Bacillus, Corynebacterium or Streptomyces hosts for recombinant proteins, enzymes, amino acids and precision-fermentation ingredients.
problem: Phage contamination can cause widespread fermentation failure and lingering facility contamination, and outages are usually hidden. Dairy lactic-acid strains have phage-resistance programs, but most other production hosts do not. Academic work shows phage-resistant E. coli is feasible (Nature Communications 2022; CRISPR-immunity work in 2025), yet nobody sells it as a service.
solution: (1) Surveillance: metagenomic sequencing of broth and environmental swabs for phage signatures. (2) Red team: isolate and evolve escape phages against the customer's strain in a BSL-1/2 lab, extending the search with AI-designed phage genomes. (3) Hardening: stack defense modules (restriction-modification, CRISPR, abortive infection), test them, and deliver a strain with unchanged titer.
why_now: Arc Institute and Stanford used Evo genome language models to write phage genomes: 16 viable phages from about 300 designs, and a cocktail that cleared E. coli resistant to the natural template. DNA synthesis costs have collapsed, so testing dozens of defense combinations is cheap. Precision fermentation and biologic capacity is scaling.
revenue_model: $2-6k/month per site for surveillance, $25-60k per red-team audit, and $150-400k per hardened strain as a license fee without royalties.
non_obvious_insight: Phage risk is treated as bad luck. Treating it like cybersecurity, with continuous monitoring plus adversarial testing, creates a budget line. Operators hide outages, so the first buyers are CDMO QA leads and insurers who need proof of resilience.
first_30_days: Offer a free phage-susceptibility screen of environmental swabs to 5 precision-fermentation startups. Build a library of 30 defense modules for E. coli and Bacillus. Sign 2 paid audits ($15-25k). Complete a biosafety review of the adversarial-phage protocol.

title: Dead-Lead Exchange for Solar Installers
one_liner: A reason-coded exchange where solar installers sell their disqualified leads (bad roof, shade, small panel) to roofers, arborists and electricians, with a bounty when the homeowner comes back to buy solar.
customer: Roofers, tree services and panel-upgrade electricians pay per lead. Solar installers receive a revenue share and are the supply side. The end payer is the trade at $60-150 per lead, plus a 5-10% bounty from the installer when a returned lead signs.
problem: Installers pay $100-250 for an exclusive lead and $150-800 for a booked appointment, and CAC is reportedly rising about 40% in 2026. Most of the spend dies at qualification on roof age, shade, roof type or a 100A panel, and the lead is thrown away or resold as an aged inquiry. Meanwhile roofers pay hundreds per closed lead for homeowners who may not need a roof at all.
solution: Installers connect their CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, JobNimbus, Enerflo) through a webhook. Every lead tagged with a disqualification reason goes to the exchange. A fresh, named-trade consent step, by SMS or a call, offers the homeowner a free quote from a local roofer to make the house solar-ready. The exchange sells the lead to a matched local trade with the diagnosis attached: roof age, photos, shade map, utility bill. When the work completes, the lead returns to the original installer with a 90-day exclusive hold, and the installer pays a bounty if it closes.
why_now: After 25D expired, installers are fighting over unit economics and CAC is climbing, so recouping 30-50% of lead cost matters. Roofers face slower storm work. Homeowners still want solar through TPO, which typically requires 10-15+ years of roof life, so more leads get rejected on roof grounds.
revenue_model: Take 50-60% of the lead price with the rest shared with the installer. Add a 5-10% bounty on returned solar sales. Add a per-seat subscription for roofing and tree companies to get first look in their zip codes. Later, add a financing product that bundles a roof and solar into one loan.
non_obvious_insight: The dead solar lead is one of the best roofing leads in the county. This is a homeowner who was ready to commit five figures to their house, has shown a utility bill, and has just been told by a credible outsider that the roof needs work, so the diagnosis is trusted. VCs treat lead-gen as a commodity, but a closed loop with bounce-back and reason codes is not. The compliance layer (fresh, named-trade consent) is the moat.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers in one metro who each have 200+ disqualified leads a month. Recruit 3 roofers and 1-2 tree services. Run the whole loop with a spreadsheet, SMS consent scripts and Stripe payouts. Price the first leads at $75-100. Track lead-to-roof-job conversion and how many come back to solar.

title: Agent Purchase Warranty: The Liability Layer
one_liner: Everyone is building payment rails for shopping agents. Nobody owns what happens when an agent buys the wrong thing, so sell the warranty and dispute layer.
customer: Startups building AI procurement and shopping agents for small businesses (office, restaurant and parts supplies), and the merchants those agents buy from. The first buyer is an agent vendor that wants merchants to accept its agent.
problem: Visa, Mastercard, Coinbase, Ripple and Stripe are all in agentic rails, and Visa and Mastercard joined Rain's alliance on 2026-08-18. Chargeback rules assume a human clicked buy. ISO's generative-AI exclusion is spreading across CGL policies, so when an agent orders 40 cases instead of 4, the merchant says it was authorized, the bank agrees, and the insurer excludes it.
solution: A mandate-versus-receipt adjudication API. The user's signed intent mandate (budget, item class, merchant allowlist) is logged. On a dispute, the API compares mandate, cart, receipt and delivery and pays valid claims automatically. The first version is a reserve-backed service warranty capped at $500-$2,000 per order, later fronted by an MGA and carrier. Merchants who accept mandate-logged agent orders get a 'warranted agent' signal that cuts false declines.
why_now: Agentic payments alliances formed in Aug 2026, DoorDash is live on Stripe/Tempo, and AI exclusions are appearing on thousands of CGL policies (Insurance Business, 2026-09-16). Transaction volume is arriving just as coverage disappears.
revenue_model: Per-order warranty fee of about 0.4-1.0% of order value from the agent vendor or user. Merchant-side acceptance fee. Later, MGA commission once a carrier fronts the risk.
non_obvious_insight: Rails are commodity and crowded, but liability allocation is what decides trust, just as Stripe won by absorbing fraud and disputes rather than moving bytes. Insurers exclude 'AI' generically because they have no data. A signed mandate log is exactly the data that lets a small underwriter price a slice they can't.
first_30_days: Pick one SMB-procurement agent vendor. Offer a free mandate-log SDK plus a capped $50k reserve-backed warranty on its first 500 orders, and record dispute types and rates. Use that loss data to sign three similar vendors at about 0.75% per order.

title: Orphan Bin Network: Leased Farm Storage Capacity
one_liner: Lease the thousands of idle grain bins left on consolidated and inherited farmsteads, retrofit them with cheap sensors, and run them as licensed satellite storage for co-ops.
customer: Co-ops and independent elevators that run short of upright storage every big harvest. Also landlord and heir bin owners who receive lease income. The elevator pays a per-bin SaaS fee plus a share of storage revenue.
problem: Upright storage is the co-op's hardest constraint, and building new capacity costs a huge multiple of leasing existing steel. Ground piles cost shrink and quality. Meanwhile farm consolidation and aging landowners leave many bins idle on rented farmsteads. Heirs pay taxes on stranded assets and have no way to monetize them. Iowa law already contemplates leased storage facilities under a warehouse license (the licensee simply notifies the state), but no one has packaged the monitoring, inventory verification and paperwork to make it routine.
solution: A 'bin-in-a-box' program run under the co-op's existing warehouse license. Sign multi-year leases with owners and install a retrofit kit: temperature and moisture cables, fill-level sensors, aeration control and a remote camera. Wire it into the co-op's grain accounting system so receipts, inventory and shrink tracking work like any owned bin. Provide the compliance package (state notifications, insurance riders, inspection logs, an auditor-ready trail). This is not a marketplace. The co-op stays the licensed warehouseman and the bin owner becomes a landlord.
why_now: The 2025 record harvest left the top 12 corn states about 1.4 billion bushels short of upright storage, according to CoBank analysis, and low prices keep grain in storage longer. Elevators piled grain on the ground and rented temporary space. Cheap LoRa and cellular bin sensors now cost far less than a few years ago, and 2026 harvest is starting.
revenue_model: SaaS of about $250 to $500 per bin per year plus install margin on the sensor kit. 10% to 20% share of incremental storage revenue. Optional financing spread on kit costs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not steel but licensed, monitored, insurable steel. Idle bins already exist by the thousands. What is missing is the trust layer (sensors, chain-of-custody and a bonded warehouseman) that lets an elevator sign for grain sitting in someone else's yard.
first_30_days: Pick one co-op that just piled grain on the ground. Identify 10 idle bins within 15 miles from the co-op's landlord and ag-lending contacts. Confirm the notification steps with the Iowa Grain Warehouse Bureau. Install sensor kits on 5 bins before harvest peak and store real grain for the first time this season.

title: Film Camera Repair Guild and Parts Mill
one_liner: A training-plus-parts network that multiplies the number of people able to repair 1970s-90s film cameras, using 3D-printed and machined parts and paid video teardown courses.
customer: Independent repair techs and serious hobbyists (parts kits and courses), used-camera shops and labs (bulk repaired-and-warrantied stock), and consumers via mail-in.
problem: The film revival is real but repairers are retiring (ABC News Dec 2025; PetaPixel Jan 2026), many now refuse to service certain models, and mechanical parts are hard to source. Dead cameras mean lost film buyers.
solution: Start with the ~25 most popular bodies (AE-1, K1000, X-700, FM2 and similar). Sell light-seal, mirror-bumper and foam kits plus printed or CNC-machined gears. Publish paid step-by-step repair courses, certify guild repairers, route overflow mail-in jobs to them, and sell warrantied repaired stock wholesale to used shops.
why_now: The retirement wave is now documented in mainstream press. Cheap multi-material printing and on-demand metal parts vendors exist. Film demand keeps rising among under-35s, and used-camera prices are climbing.
revenue_model: Parts kits ($8-40), course subscriptions (~$20/month), a ~25% share of routed repairs, and wholesale of repaired cameras with warranty.
non_obvious_insight: Film-industry insiders assume the constraint on the revival is film stock and new cameras. It is repair capacity: repair knowledge is tacit and walking out the door. Apprenticeship packaged as content, plus a parts supply, is the picks-and-shovels play, and every dead SLR is a lost film customer.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken AE-1 and K1000 lots on eBay and film every teardown. Sell foam and seal kits on Etsy and eBay with instructions. Pre-sell 100 lifetime course seats to r/AnalogCommunity. Recruit 3 retiring techs as paid instructors on revenue share.

title: Ceremony-as-a-Service for Direct Cremation Providers
one_liner: White-label the memorial gathering that low-cost cremation providers can't deliver, so families buy a $1.5K box of ashes plus a $3.5K send-off.
customer: Direct-cremation companies (online and storefront), hospices and community organizations. Families pay for the events.
problem: NFDA projects cremation at 63.4% in 2025, rising to 82.3% by 2045. Direct-cremation providers win on price but hand families ashes with no ceremony. Consolidators' chapels and $8K packages don't fit that customer. NFDA reports 58.3% of consumers have attended services at unconventional venues, so demand exists but no one owns the coordination.
solution: A 'Celebration Desk' embedded in the provider's checkout as 'add a gathering'. A coordinator plus software books non-funeral venues (breweries, restaurants, parks, boats, halls), catering, a celebrant, a slideshow, live-stream and RSVPs. Packages are fixed-price at $1,500, $3,500 or $7,500. It also handles scattering permits and follow-up.
why_now: Direct cremation share keeps climbing. NFDA says 61.4% of consumers are interested in green options. Consolidators are structurally pinned to a 58% cremation mix and 3%+ annual price increases and cannot copy an unbundled model. Venues have empty weekday capacity and live-streaming is now trivial.
revenue_model: Fixed package fee at 35-45% gross margin, 10-15% rev share from venues and caterers, and a referral or white-label fee of $150-$300 per booked event to the cremation provider.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see direct cremation as the industry's price-war threat. It is really an unbundling that turned the ceremony into a separate, high-margin purchase that nobody owns. The providers who created it have no event staff, and the consolidators' chapels are the wrong shape.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign one direct-cremation provider and ten venues. Coordinate the first five events by hand at about $1,800 each, offered through the provider's post-arrangement email. Photograph and price each event to build the package catalog.

title: Whey-Free Calf Milk Replacer
one_liner: Sell alternative-protein milk replacer to calf raisers hit by whey prices, where functionality demands are far looser than in food.
customer: Calf ranches, dairy heifer raisers, beef-on-dairy operations and regional feed mills.
problem: Calf milk replacers lean on whey protein, whose price is up 108% in two years, squeezing the operations that supply beef-on-dairy calves at the moment the herd is at a 75-year low.
solution: A milk replacer built on potato, pea, hydrolyzed and fermentation-derived proteins plus a tuned fat blend, with growth-trial performance guarantees.
why_now: Whey has become scarcer than the cheese it came from, and record calf values make feed cost per pound of gain a live issue.
revenue_model: Bag sales per pound plus per-head feeding programs with performance guarantees.
non_obvious_insight: Sell alternative proteins to animals first: feed has no clear-drink functionality bar and the buyer measures ROI in daily gain rather than taste.
first_30_days: Hire a ruminant nutritionist, run a feeding trial at two calf ranches, and offer pilot programs priced per pound of gain.

title: Layoff Early-Warning for Credit Unions
one_liner: Turns public WARN notices and layoff signals into member-level outreach lists, so lenders can offer hardship plans about 60 days before payments are missed.
customer: Credit unions (roughly 4,400 in the US), community banks, mortgage servicers and auto lenders pay $1.5-6k a month, often via credit-union service organisations.
problem: White-collar layoffs are lumpy and local (information-sector employment fell 23k in one Aug 2026 month, Amazon cut ~16,000 corporate roles). Lenders learn about them from missed payments, when charge-off risk is already high and members are hardest to help. Hardship programs exist but outreach comes too late.
solution: Ingest state WARN databases, news and layoff trackers. Match employers to the lender's book using payroll ACH descriptors on member accounts. Rank members by exposure, then supply compliant outreach scripts, pre-approved skip-a-pay or modification offers, and uplift measurement.
why_now: Layoffs are steady and concentrated in higher-balance, AI-exposed white-collar borrowers. Payroll descriptors and open-banking data make the join easy. Small lenders have no data teams, and the low-hire market makes re-employment slow (7-13 months in practitioner reports).
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-6k a month per institution, or a performance fee on avoided delinquencies.
non_obvious_insight: The layoffs are public. The scarce piece is the join to the lender's book via payroll descriptors. Employees of a laid-off employer often bank at the same local credit union, so the risk is concentrated, and the ROI is stated in avoided charge-offs rather than charity.
first_30_days: Normalise 50 state WARN sources. Backtest with a friendly credit union on two past layoff events to show missed payments 45-90 days later. Get two credit-union service organisations to run a paid $1k-a-month pilot.

title: Supply-House-Branded Back Office for Tiny Shops
one_liner: White-label quote, invoice, parts-pricing and trade-credit software delivered to solo-to-5-tech shops through their local independent supply house counter.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical and roofing supply houses and regional distributors squeezed by Home Depot (SRS, GMS, Mingledorff's) and Lowe's (FBM, Artisan). End users are their trade account holders.
problem: ServiceTitan fell about 26% after Q2 on slowing GTV, softer HVAC leads and a delay on exteriors, and expects only about 700 locations on its agentic tier. Most tiny shops have no operations layer and will not buy software cold, since CAC is brutal and churn high. Independent distributors are losing pro accounts to big-box integration and need a reason for contractors to stay.
solution: A private-label 'contractor OS' under the distributor's brand. Quotes are built from the distributor's live price book, invoices are text-to-pay, job notes and callbacks are tracked, truck stock reorders route to the counter, and net-30 parts credit is bundled. Counter staff onboard shops in person. It is free with a trade account, and the distributor pays per active shop.
why_now: Home Depot bought Mingledorff's in May 2026 on top of SRS and GMS, and Lowe's bought FBM for $8.8B. Independents' backs are against the wall. ServiceTitan's drop and deprioritization of exteriors leave small shops ignored. LLM-assisted development makes a lightweight tool cheap to build.
revenue_model: $30-60 per active shop per month paid by the distributor, or 0.25-0.5% of the shop's parts spend. Add payments interchange share and parts-financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Vertical software wins on distribution. The supply house counter is the one place every tiny shop shows up every week, and distributors have both a strategic reason (defense against big-box) and a budget to pay for stickiness. Contractors will adopt anything that makes parts pricing and credit easier.
first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses through buying-group contacts. Build an MVP on price-book CSV upload, SMS quotes and Stripe. Pilot with 20 shops per distributor and measure parts spend lift per shop.

title: RouteRx: Pharmacy Delivery on Co-op Fuel Routes
one_liner: Piggyback prescription and essentials delivery onto the propane, fuel and feed routes that already pass most rural households, so surviving independent pharmacies can serve people the chains just abandoned.
customer: Independent rural pharmacies (per-delivery fee), Medicare Advantage and Part D plans and rural health clinics (per-member adherence and wellness-check fee), and the co-op energy department, which keeps a share of route revenue.
problem: Rite Aid is gone, Walgreens is closing about 1,200 stores through 2027, and more than 2,000 US pharmacies closed in 2025 alone. Rural residents, especially older ones on propane and well water, are hours from a counter. Standalone courier delivery in a county of 12,000 people costs $15 to $30 a drop in deadhead miles. Independents cannot afford it, and plans cannot buy adherence in places with no last mile.
solution: The co-op's energy drivers already pass nearly every farmstead and acreage in a 25-mile radius on weekly or monthly cycles. They know the gate codes, where the dog is, and which customers live alone. Add a locked, tamper-evident tote and a driver app with signature capture and temperature logging. A partner pharmacy dispenses, and the driver acts as its contracted courier under existing Iowa delivery rules, with no controlled substances at first. Add optional 'no-heat and welfare check' notes that flag when a propane customer looks unwell, triggering a call to family or the clinic.
why_now: The 2025 to 2026 pharmacy shakeout has left rural pharmacy deserts, and Drug Channels' August 2026 analysis describes a K-shaped market of urban consolidation and rural lost access. Payers are looking for adherence and social-needs benefits. Co-op energy departments are under margin pressure and need new route revenue.
revenue_model: $5 to $9 per delivery from pharmacies. Medicare Advantage and Part D plan per-member-per-month adherence and check-in fees. The co-op takes a route revenue share of roughly 30%. Optional expansion to labs, groceries and parcels.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in rural health is not delivery technology but route density that is already paid for. A propane bobtail passing a home every three weeks has a near-zero marginal stop cost, and it carries something no courier startup has, which is trust from decades of showing up.
first_30_days: Sign one co-op with an LP fleet and one independent pharmacy in an adjacent town that just lost a competitor. Get a written read from the Iowa Board of Pharmacy and the co-op's insurer. Run a 20-household pilot with tamper-evident bags and an off-the-shelf delivery app. Record cost per stop and refill adherence to pitch a regional Medicare Advantage plan.

title: Camera Sentinels for Screwworm on Ranches
one_liner: Solar cameras at water troughs and chutes that flag wounded animals early, so ranchers can act before quarantine.
customer: Texas and Southern cattle ranchers, feedyards and stockyards, plus livestock insurers.
problem: New World screwworm is confirmed in Texas cattle and wound checks on huge pastures are impossible with scarce labor, while one missed case can trigger quarantine and lost sales.
solution: Cellular solar cameras with computer vision fine-tuned on wound and head-shaking images, alerts with geotags, and exportable inspection logs to support movement documentation.
why_now: Confirmed screwworm in Texas, a Mexican feeder-cattle halt removing about 1.2M head a year, and record cattle values make early detection worth real money.
revenue_model: $40-90 per camera per month plus installation, with possible insurer and state-program subsidies.
non_obvious_insight: You are selling regulatory insurance rather than analytics: the asymmetry of one undetected case versus a daily-check labor bill makes even a noisy sentinel valuable.
first_30_days: Install about 20 off-the-shelf trail cameras on five Texas ranches, collect wound imagery with local vets, and run a 30-day alert pilot billed per camera.
